client: I've been having a really hard time at family get-togethers ever since my grandmother passed away six months ago. Everyone else seems to just... move on, laughing and talking like nothing changed, and I'm sitting there feeling completely hollow inside. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because nothing anyone says seems to bring her back or make those gatherings feel normal again.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — that hollow feeling in the middle of a room full of laughter can be one of the loneliest experiences there is, and it makes complete sense that six months isn't nearly enough time to feel "normal" again after losing someone so important to you. You're right that nothing anyone says will bring her back, and I want you to know I'm not here to offer you a fix — just a space to be honest about what this has been like. I'm wondering, when you're sitting at those gatherings feeling hollow, what thoughts tend to run through your mind about what it *means* that others seem to have moved on?

client: Mostly I think it means they didn't love her the way I did, or maybe that I'm the only one who really understood how much she held everything together. And then I feel guilty for even thinking that, because I know that's probably not fair to them. It just makes me feel even more alone, like I'm grieving in a completely different language than everyone else in the room.
therapist: That image of "grieving in a different language" is so beautifully and painfully accurate — it captures how isolating it feels when your inner world and the room around you seem completely disconnected. It's also really worth noticing that you're already questioning that thought about your family, which takes a kind of emotional honesty that isn't easy, especially when you're hurting this much. I'm curious — when you think about your grandmother and how much she meant to you, is there any part of you that can imagine she might have had a similarly unique, irreplaceable bond with even one other person in that room?

client: I mean... yeah, my aunt probably. She and my grandmother talked on the phone every single day, and I know that because my grandmother used to mention it. But honestly, even thinking about that makes me feel a strange kind of jealousy, like acknowledging her grief somehow takes something away from mine, which I know sounds awful.
therapist: It doesn't sound awful at all — it sounds deeply human, and the fact that you can name that jealousy so honestly is actually a sign of real self-awareness rather than something to be ashamed of. Grief can feel like the last place where we still *have* the person we lost, so sharing it can unconsciously feel like losing them all over again. I wonder what it might feel like to gently imagine, just as an experiment, approaching your aunt at the next gathering and asking her one small thing about your grandmother — not to compete in grief, but to speak even a few words of that same language with someone who might understand it?

client: That actually makes a lot of sense, what you said about grief being the last place I still have her. But I'm worried that if I bring her up with my aunt, one of us is going to fall apart, and then everyone else at the gathering will feel uncomfortable or try to change the subject, and it'll just make me feel more isolated than if I'd said nothing at all. It feels safer to just stay quiet and carry it alone, even though I know that's not really working either.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — you can see clearly that staying quiet isn't working, and yet reaching out feels risky too, which means you're caught between two kinds of pain rather than a safe option and a scary one. That fear of "falling apart" together is worth examining gently, though — is it possible that two people crying over someone they both loved deeply is actually the most natural thing in the world, even if others in the room feel briefly uncomfortable? I'm wondering, when you imagine that moment of vulnerability with your aunt, is the discomfort you're most afraid of *hers*, *yours*, or the feeling of being witnessed by the others around you?

client: Honestly, I think it's mostly about being witnessed by the others. Like, if it were just me and my aunt alone somewhere, I think I could handle it, but the idea of breaking down in front of everyone and then having them all look at me with that pitying expression... it makes me want to disappear. I guess I've always had this thing where showing that much emotion in front of people feels like losing control, and losing control in public feels almost worse than the grief itself.
therapist: That's a really significant insight — the grief itself isn't what feels unbearable, it's the vulnerability of being *seen* in it by people whose reactions you can't control, which tells us something important about where the real weight is coming from. It sounds like somewhere along the way you learned that showing deep emotion in front of others isn't safe, and that belief is now standing between you and the one thing that might actually ease your loneliness. I'm curious — when you imagine someone else breaking down at a gathering out of love for your grandmother, would you look at them with pity, or would you feel something closer to recognition and tenderness?

client: I'd feel tenderness, obviously, and probably relief that someone else was feeling it too. But I think that's the thing that's hard to sit with, because it means I'm probably being unfair to myself in a way I wouldn't be to anyone else. It's just so much easier to extend that kind of compassion to other people than to believe that I deserve the same thing from the people in that room.
therapist: You just did something really profound — you caught yourself applying a completely different standard to yourself than you would to someone you love, and naming that gap *is* the first step toward closing it. That tendency to be a harsh judge of yourself while being a tender witness to others is something we can absolutely work with together. I'd like to ask you to sit with this for a moment: if your grandmother were in that room and she saw you grieving her, what do you imagine her expression would look like?

client: She would have looked at me with so much love, I know that without even having to think about it. She was always the one person who made me feel like my feelings were never too much, never embarrassing, just... valid. And sitting with that right now is making my chest ache in a way that feels different from the hollow feeling, almost like it hurts more but in a way that's somehow more real.
therapist: That ache you're feeling right now is grief in one of its most honest forms — it hurts more because you're actually *with* her for a moment, rather than just feeling her absence, and that's a very different and important kind of pain. What strikes me deeply is that the unconditional acceptance you're longing for in that room — the feeling that your emotions are never too much — is something she already gave you, and in some ways it still lives in you because she put it there. I'm wondering if, in those moments at family gatherings when you feel most alone, there might be a way to gently ask yourself what she would say to you if she could see you sitting there carrying all of this so quietly by yourself?

client: She would have told me to stop being so hard on myself, probably in that gentle but firm way she had, and maybe that I was allowed to miss her out loud. But I'm not sure I can actually access that in the moment when I'm sitting there feeling hollow, because it's like the grief crowds out everything else and I can't think clearly enough to ask myself anything. It's a nice idea, but I worry it'll just feel like a hollow exercise when I'm actually in the middle of it.
therapist: That's a really honest and important pushback, and you're right that insight in a calm moment doesn't automatically translate into access when you're flooded with emotion — that's not a personal failing, that's just how grief and our nervous systems actually work. What might help is creating something small and concrete *before* you're in that moment, almost like leaving yourself a note from this version of you — even something as simple as a single phrase she used to say, kept somewhere you could quietly glance at. I'm wondering, is there something specific she used to say to you — a particular word or expression that was distinctly *hers* — that might be small enough to carry with you without feeling like a big exercise?

client: She used to call me "her heart" in our language, which sounds small but it was something she only ever said to me, never to anyone else as far as I know. Just thinking about it right now is making my throat tight in a way that feels both painful and somehow precious at the same time. I guess I'm worried that if I write it down or put it on my phone, it'll start to feel mechanical or worn out, like it loses something by being turned into a coping strategy instead of just... hers.
therapist: That word is sacred, and your instinct to protect it makes complete sense — some things are too precious to be laminated into a technique, and honoring that feeling is itself a form of love for her. But I want to gently offer another way of seeing it: that word didn't belong to a strategy, it belonged to *you*, specifically and only you, and no amount of remembering it can wear that out or make it less true. I'm wondering if the worry that it might become "mechanical" is perhaps another way of that harsher inner voice suggesting you don't quite deserve to keep something so beautiful close to you whenever you need it?

client: That landed harder than I expected, because I think you might be right and I really don't want you to be. It's like there's a part of me that feels I should keep suffering through those gatherings quietly as some kind of proof that I loved her enough, and actually allowing myself comfort feels almost like a betrayal of how much I miss her. I've never quite put it together that way before, but sitting with it now, it feels uncomfortably true.
therapist: What you just articulated — that suffering has become a way of proving love — is one of the most important things you could have uncovered, and the discomfort of recognizing it is actually a sign that something real just shifted for you. Your grandmother, the woman who called you "her heart" and made you feel your feelings were never too much, I don't think she would recognize your love through your suffering — I think she already knew it completely, and would want you to know that accepting comfort and missing her fiercely can exist in the same breath. I'm wondering, if loving her and allowing yourself gentleness aren't actually opposites, what might it feel like to carry her name for you not as a coping tool, but simply as a reminder of what she already knew to be true about you?
